stem: A 34-year-old stable on levothyroxine starts a combined estrogen contraceptive. Eight weeks later she is tired and her TSH has risen. She takes her tablet correctly on an empty stomach. What explains this?

options.A: Estrogen raises thyroid-binding globulin, so her need rises
options.B: Estrogen causes hyperthyroidism, as amiodarone can
options.C: Estrogen binds levothyroxine in the gut like calcium
options.D: Estrogen induces CYP enzymes that clear levothyroxine
options.E: Estrogen blocks conversion of T4 to T3 in the tissues

why: Estrogens raise thyroid-binding globulin, so levothyroxine needs rise.

whys.B: Her TSH is high: she needs more hormone.
whys.C: Binding in the gut is calcium, iron and antacids.
whys.D: The inducers taught are rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine.
whys.E: That is PTU, iodine and steroids in storm.

takeaway: New estrogen on levothyroxine: expect a higher dose.
discriminator: More binding protein, not less absorption.

stem: A 63-year-old with type 2 diabetes on basal insulin starts prednisone 40 mg daily for a COPD flare. Which plan is most appropriate?

options.A: Hold insulin; prednisone replaces its metabolic effect
options.B: Stop prednisone abruptly at day 5 to protect the axis
options.C: Expect hypoglycemia and halve the insulin during the course
options.D: Expect hyperglycemia and adjust insulin during the course
options.E: Add spironolactone to prevent steroid hyperkalemia

why: Steroid adverse effects include hyperglycemia; insulin and oral agents need adjusting during steroid therapy.

whys.A: It opposes insulin's effect on glucose.
whys.B: Abrupt stops are the risk after long courses, and this is not the issue asked.
whys.C: Steroids raise glucose.
whys.E: Hyperkalemia is not the steroid problem here.

takeaway: Steroid course in a diabetic: plan for higher glucose.
discriminator: The steroid changes the insulin need.

stem: A 52-year-old with acromegaly has taken octreotide for a year. IGF-1 is at goal. He now reports episodes of right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals and a resting pulse of 52. Which explanation fits best?

options.A: Cabergoline effect: orthostatic hypotension and nausea
options.B: Tumor growth: the pituitary mass is pressing locally
options.C: Desmopressin effect: hyponatremia from retained water
options.D: Expected octreotide effects: gallstones and bradycardia
options.E: Pegvisomant toxicity: liver injury needing liver tests

why: Octreotide and lanreotide cause GI upset, gallstones and bradycardia (and glucose changes). Biliary pain plus a slow pulse in a controlled patient is the drug, not the disease.

whys.A: Those are dopamine-agonist effects, not his drug.
whys.B: IGF-1 is at goal and the symptoms are biliary.
whys.C: He is not on desmopressin and has no sodium symptoms.
whys.E: He takes octreotide; liver tests are the pegvisomant concern.

takeaway: Somatostatin analogs: gallstones, GI upset, bradycardia.
discriminator: Octreotide → gallbladder and pulse; pegvisomant → liver tests.

stem: A 74-year-old woman has had her levothyroxine increased three times for fatigue. TSH is now suppressed. She has new palpitations and an irregular pulse. Which risks follow from this dosing?

options.A: Agranulocytosis and liver injury from over-replacement
options.B: Atrial fibrillation and bone loss from over-replacement
options.C: Hyponatremia and seizures from retained free water
options.D: Gallstones and bradycardia from the higher dose
options.E: Adrenal crisis from suppression of CRH and ACTH

why: Over-replacement causes tachycardia, atrial fibrillation and bone loss. Dose to TSH, not to fatigue alone.

whys.A: Those are thionamide warnings.
whys.C: That is desmopressin.
whys.D: Those are octreotide effects.
whys.E: That follows chronic steroids.

takeaway: Suppressed TSH on levothyroxine: heart and bone at risk.
discriminator: Symptoms did not justify the dose; the TSH shows the excess.

stem: A 55-year-old on basal-bolus insulin starts metoprolol after a myocardial infarction. Which counseling point is most important?

options.A: Metoprolol causes euglycemic DKA, so hold insulin when ill
options.B: Glucagon no longer works, so only dextrose can be used
options.C: Warning symptoms may be masked; check glucose, rule of 15
options.D: Hypoglycemia cannot occur on a beta-blocker, so relax targets
options.E: Metoprolol raises insulin levels, so halve every insulin dose

why: Beta-blockers can mask hypoglycemia warning symptoms. Treat a low with 15 g of carbohydrate and recheck in 15 minutes; glucagon or dextrose rescue severe hypoglycemia.

whys.A: That is the SGLT2-inhibitor warning.
whys.B: Both remain rescue options for severe lows.
whys.D: It can occur and may go unnoticed.
whys.E: The taught effect is masking, not a level change.

takeaway: Insulin + beta-blocker: lows can be silent.
discriminator: Masked symptoms vs a changed drug level.

stem: A 71-year-old started desmopressin for central diabetes insipidus 10 days ago. To 'stay hydrated' he drinks water all day. He is now confused with a headache and nausea. Which step is most appropriate first?

options.A: Check serum sodium for desmopressin hyponatremia
options.B: Start demeclocycline to counter the retained water
options.C: Raise the desmopressin dose for incomplete control
options.D: Check liver tests for desmopressin hepatotoxicity
options.E: Add tolvaptan to speed water excretion at home

why: Desmopressin keeps free water in. The risk is hyponatremia, so sodium is monitored and fluids are limited.

whys.B: Demeclocycline is a refractory-SIADH option.
whys.C: More drug would retain more water.
whys.D: Liver injury is the tolvaptan concern.
whys.E: Tolvaptan is for SIADH and is started in hospital.

takeaway: Desmopressin: monitor sodium, limit fluids.
discriminator: Desmopressin → hyponatremia; tolvaptan → overcorrection and liver injury.

stem: A 39-year-old with Cushing syndrome and type 2 diabetes starts mifepristone. A month later her glucose control is better, but serum cortisol is higher than before. Which interpretation is correct?

options.A: Adrenal crisis: give IV hydrocortisone and fluids now
options.B: Expected with receptor block: follow clinically, check K⁺
options.C: Expected: also check PSA, which the drug lowers by half
options.D: Treatment failure: switch to ketoconazole to lower cortisol
options.E: Lab error: cortisol always falls on a receptor blocker

why: Mifepristone blocks the glucocorticoid receptor. Cortisol levels rise, so response is judged clinically. It causes hypokalemia and is contraindicated in pregnancy.

whys.A: She is improving; nothing suggests crisis.
whys.C: That is the finasteride rule.
whys.D: Cortisol rises with receptor blockade; levels mislead.
whys.E: Cortisol levels rise on mifepristone.

takeaway: Mifepristone: cortisol goes up, so watch the patient and potassium.
discriminator: Synthesis blockers lower cortisol; a receptor blocker does not.

stem: A patient with acromegaly switches from octreotide to pegvisomant. Three months later IGF-1 is normal, but MRI shows the adenoma unchanged in size. Which statement explains both findings?

options.A: It restores dopamine tone, so prolactin and GH both fall
options.B: It blocks the GH receptor: IGF-1 falls, tumor untouched
options.C: It replaces GH, so feedback switches the adenoma off
options.D: It blocks IGF-1 itself, so GH and the tumor are suppressed
options.E: It lowers GH release, so the tumor should shrink with time

why: Pegvisomant blocks the GH receptor, so the liver makes less IGF-1. It does not act on the pituitary, so it does not shrink the tumor; monitor IGF-1 and liver tests.

whys.A: That describes cabergoline in prolactinoma.
whys.C: Somatropin replaces GH and is for deficiency.
whys.D: Its target is the GH receptor, not IGF-1.
whys.E: That describes octreotide and lanreotide.

takeaway: Pegvisomant fixes the lab, not the tumor.
discriminator: Octreotide lowers GH release; pegvisomant blocks its receptor.

stem: A 78-year-old with coronary artery disease and new hypothyroidism (TSH 14 mIU/L) is starting levothyroxine. Which plan is safest?

options.A: Start a full dose and recheck TSH in 1 week
options.B: Start a low dose taken with calcium at breakfast
options.C: Start a low dose and recheck TSH at 6–8 weeks
options.D: Start a full dose and titrate to a suppressed TSH
options.E: Delay treatment until the TSH rises above 20 mIU/L

why: Start low in older adults and in cardiac disease, then check TSH at 6–8 weeks. Over-replacement causes tachycardia, atrial fibrillation and bone loss.

whys.A: Older and cardiac patients start low; TSH needs 6–8 weeks.
whys.B: Calcium reduces absorption; separate by 4 hours.
whys.D: Over-replacement risks tachycardia, AF and bone loss.
whys.E: The lecture teaches start low, not withhold.

takeaway: Old or cardiac: start low, TSH at 6–8 weeks.
discriminator: Under-treating is slow; over-replacing hits the heart and bone.

stem: A 41-year-old with untreated Graves disease arrives with fever 40°C, heart rate 158, agitation and vomiting after an infection. Propranolol has been given. Which sequence is correct for the next drugs?

options.A: Iodine now, PTU 1 hour after it, plus hydrocortisone
options.B: Methimazole now, with levothyroxine held until afterwards
options.C: PTU now, aspirin for the fever, then iodine an hour later
options.D: PTU now, iodine an hour after it, plus hydrocortisone
options.E: Hydrocortisone alone, since it blocks all hormone release

why: Beta-blocker and PTU come first; iodine is given only after PTU because iodine first would feed new hormone synthesis. Steroids blunt peripheral conversion and cover relative adrenal insufficiency. Aspirin is avoided.

whys.A: Iodine before PTU supplies substrate for new hormone.
whys.B: The storm sequence taught is PTU first, then iodine.
whys.C: Aspirin frees bound hormone and is avoided in storm.
whys.E: Steroids help conversion and adrenal cover; they are added.

takeaway: Storm order: beta-blocker + PTU, then iodine, plus steroid.
discriminator: PTU blocks synthesis; iodine blocks release, but only after PTU.

stem: A 24-year-old on a combined oral contraceptive starts rifampin for 4 months. She asks whether her pill still works. Which advice is correct?

options.A: Switch to levothyroxine timing rules: separate by 4 hours
options.B: Rifampin lowers hormone levels; use backup contraception
options.C: Rifampin raises estrogen levels; watch for clots instead
options.D: No change is needed; only St. John's wort matters
options.E: Double the pill dose and no backup method is needed

why: Enzyme inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St. John's wort) lower contraceptive efficacy; use backup contraception.

whys.A: Separation fixes binding, not enzyme induction.
whys.C: Inducers lower hormone levels.
whys.D: Rifampin is a named inducer, as is St. John's wort.
whys.E: The lecture's answer is backup contraception.

takeaway: Inducer + pill = backup method.
discriminator: Induction lowers levels; it cannot be fixed by spacing doses.

stem: A 66-year-old has taken finasteride for 2 years. His screening PSA is 2.4 ng/mL. How should this value be read?

options.A: As about 4.8 ng/mL, because finasteride halves PSA
options.B: As about 4.8 ng/mL, because testosterone raises PSA
options.C: As 2.4 ng/mL, because finasteride does not change PSA
options.D: As uninterpretable, so PSA screening should stop
options.E: As about 1.2 ng/mL, because finasteride doubles PSA

why: Finasteride lowers PSA by about half, so the measured value is doubled when screening.

whys.B: He is on finasteride, not testosterone.
whys.C: Finasteride lowers PSA by about half.
whys.D: The value is still usable once doubled.
whys.E: It lowers PSA; the correction is to double.

takeaway: On finasteride, double the PSA.
discriminator: Finasteride lowers PSA; testosterone therapy needs PSA monitored.

stem: A 49-year-old with obesity and type 2 diabetes asks for semaglutide. Her brother had medullary thyroid cancer and she has had pancreatitis. She takes sitagliptin. Which statement is most complete?

options.A: Safe to start alongside sitagliptin for a stronger effect
options.B: Safe to start; only her own thyroid cancer would matter
options.C: Contraindicated only because it causes hypoglycemia
options.D: Contraindicated only because of heart-failure risk
options.E: Contraindicated by the family history; it also must not be added to sitagliptin

why: GLP-1 RAs carry an MTC/MEN2 contraindication, a pancreatitis risk and gallstones, and are not combined with a DPP-4 inhibitor.

whys.A: A GLP-1 RA is not combined with a DPP-4 inhibitor.
whys.B: MTC or MEN2 history is the contraindication taught.
whys.C: Its release of insulin is glucose-dependent.
whys.D: That is the TZD concern.

takeaway: GLP-1 RA: ask about MTC/MEN2, pancreatitis, and a DPP-4 inhibitor.
discriminator: Three separate stops in one history.

stem: A 34-year-old with gastroparesis has taken metoclopramide for 4 months. She reports galactorrhea and missed periods. Pregnancy test is negative and prolactin is elevated. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Primary hypothyroidism from an undetected drug interaction
options.B: Estrogen excess raising thyroid-binding globulin levels
options.C: A prolactinoma that now needs cabergoline twice weekly
options.D: Metoclopramide stimulates dopamine, raising prolactin release
options.E: Metoclopramide blocks dopamine, the brake on prolactin

why: Dopamine is the brake on prolactin. Antipsychotics and metoclopramide block dopamine, so prolactin rises.

whys.A: Nothing here points to thyroid drugs or disease.
whys.B: That changes levothyroxine needs, not prolactin.
whys.C: A drug cause must be excluded first; she takes a dopamine blocker.
whys.D: Dopamine inhibits prolactin; the drug blocks it.

takeaway: Dopamine blockers raise prolactin.
discriminator: Cabergoline restores the brake; metoclopramide removes it.

stem: A 45-year-old on a stable prednisone dose for sarcoidosis starts itraconazole for a fungal infection. Three weeks later she has new facial rounding, glucose 230 mg/dL and insomnia. Which mechanism is most likely?

options.A: Prednisone inhibits azole clearance, causing azole toxicity
options.B: The azole displaces steroid from thyroid-binding globulin
options.C: The azole inhibits CYP3A4, raising corticosteroid exposure
options.D: The azole induces CYP3A4, speeding steroid clearance
options.E: The azole blocks cortisol synthesis, causing deficiency

why: Azole antifungals raise corticosteroid exposure through CYP3A4. Same dose, more effect: hyperglycemia and cushingoid features.

whys.A: The taught interaction runs the other way.
whys.B: That protein is about estrogen and levothyroxine.
whys.D: Induction would lower steroid effect; rifampin does that.
whys.E: Her findings are steroid excess, not deficiency.

takeaway: Azole + steroid = more steroid effect.
discriminator: Inhibitors raise steroid exposure; rifampin, phenytoin and carbamazepine lower it.

stem: A 70-year-old on amiodarone for a year has weight gain, cold intolerance and a high TSH. A second patient on amiodarone has weight loss, tremor and a suppressed TSH. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Only the second fits: amiodarone causes hyperthyroidism only
options.B: Neither fits: lithium, not amiodarone, affects the thyroid
options.C: Both fit: amiodarone can cause hypo- or hyperthyroidism
options.D: Both fit: amiodarone raises thyroid-binding globulin
options.E: Only the first fits: amiodarone causes hypothyroidism only

why: Amiodarone and lithium can cause hypo- or hyperthyroidism.

whys.A: It can cause either.
whys.B: Both drugs are named.
whys.D: That is the estrogen mechanism.
whys.E: It can cause either.

takeaway: Amiodarone or lithium: check the thyroid, either direction.
discriminator: One drug, two opposite thyroid pictures.

stem: A 49-year-old taking tamoxifen after breast cancer is started on paroxetine for depression and hot flashes. Which concern should the PA raise?

options.A: Tamoxifen inhibits CYP2D6 and raises paroxetine levels
options.B: Paroxetine inhibits CYP2D6 and blunts tamoxifen activation
options.C: The pair causes hyperkalemia, so potassium is monitored
options.D: Paroxetine adds to tamoxifen's endometrial cancer risk
options.E: Paroxetine induces CYP3A4 and clears tamoxifen faster

why: Tamoxifen needs CYP2D6 to be activated. Paroxetine and fluoxetine inhibit CYP2D6, so less active drug is formed.

whys.A: Cinacalcet is the CYP2D6 inhibitor in this unit.
whys.C: Hyperkalemia is the spironolactone interaction.
whys.D: That risk belongs to tamoxifen alone.
whys.E: The taught interaction is CYP2D6 inhibition.

takeaway: Tamoxifen + paroxetine or fluoxetine = less activation.
discriminator: A prodrug loses effect with an inhibitor.

stem: A 57-year-old on empagliflozin has had vomiting and poor intake for 2 days. Glucose is 168 mg/dL, bicarbonate is low and ketones are positive. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Not DKA, because the glucose is under 250 mg/dL
options.B: Lactic acidosis from metformin; stop it for contrast
options.C: Sulfonylurea hypoglycemia; treat with the rule of 15
options.D: Euglycemic DKA; the drug is held during illness
options.E: Pancreatitis from the drug; check for gallstones

why: SGLT2 inhibitors cause genital yeast infections, volume depletion and euglycemic DKA. They are held when the patient is ill or before surgery.

whys.A: SGLT2 inhibitors cause DKA with near-normal glucose.
whys.B: She takes empagliflozin and has ketones.
whys.C: Glucose is 168 and she is not on a sulfonylurea.
whys.E: Pancreatitis and gallstones are GLP-1 RA concerns.

takeaway: Sick on an SGLT2 inhibitor: think DKA even with normal glucose.
discriminator: Glucose does not rule it out; ketones and bicarbonate do the work.

stem: A 72-year-old on metformin for 9 years has eGFR 27, numb feet and is booked for a contrast CT. Which set of actions matches the lecture?

options.A: Continue metformin and add a sulfonylurea for the numbness
options.B: Continue metformin, hold only for contrast, check TSH
options.C: Double metformin, since low eGFR reduces its effect
options.D: Stop metformin and start pioglitazone for the neuropathy
options.E: Stop metformin at this eGFR, hold for contrast, check B12

why: Metformin: GI upset early, vitamin B12 deficiency with long-term use, hold for contrast, avoid when eGFR is below 30.

whys.A: Numbness after long use suggests B12 deficiency.
whys.B: It is avoided when eGFR is under 30.
whys.C: Low eGFR raises risk; it does not call for more drug.
whys.D: Pioglitazone does not treat neuropathy.

takeaway: Metformin: eGFR 30, contrast, B12.
discriminator: Three separate rules that can meet in one patient.

stem: A 41-year-old with primary adrenal insufficiency takes hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone. Which monitoring belongs specifically to fludrocortisone?

options.A: Blood pressure and potassium
options.B: Sodium and fluid intake
options.C: Hematocrit and PSA
options.D: IGF-1 and liver tests
options.E: TSH at 6–8 weeks

why: Fludrocortisone: monitor blood pressure and potassium.

whys.B: That is desmopressin.
whys.C: That is testosterone.
whys.D: That is pegvisomant.
whys.E: That is levothyroxine.

takeaway: Fludrocortisone: BP and potassium.
discriminator: Each replacement hormone has its own lab.

stem: An 81-year-old on metformin has A1c above goal. She lives alone and has fallen twice this year. Which add-on fits the lecture's reasoning?

options.A: Glipizide, because it is the most potent oral option
options.B: Pioglitazone, because fluid retention protects from falls
options.C: Repaglinide, because mealtime dosing prevents all lows
options.D: Semaglutide plus sitagliptin, to cover both incretin steps
options.E: Sitagliptin, because its hypoglycemia risk is low

why: For an older adult who falls, choose the safest drug, not the most potent. Sulfonylureas force glucose-independent insulin release; a DPP-4 or SGLT2 inhibitor is preferable.

whys.A: Sulfonylureas carry the highest oral hypoglycemia risk.
whys.B: Fluid retention and heart failure are its risks.
whys.C: It is still a secretagogue.
whys.D: A GLP-1 RA is not combined with a DPP-4 inhibitor.

takeaway: Falls + diabetes: avoid sulfonylureas.
discriminator: Glucose-dependent drugs rarely cause lows; secretagogues do.

stem: A 60-year-old on repaglinide with meals starts gemfibrozil for triglycerides. A week later he has sweating and tremor before lunch on several days. What is the mechanism?

options.A: Gemfibrozil blocks DPP-4, doubling the incretin effect
options.B: Gemfibrozil induces CYP2C8 and lowers repaglinide levels
options.C: Gemfibrozil inhibits CYP2D6, as cinacalcet also does
options.D: Gemfibrozil inhibits CYP2C8 and raises repaglinide levels
options.E: Gemfibrozil masks hypoglycemia like a beta-blocker does

why: Gemfibrozil raises repaglinide levels through CYP2C8, so the secretagogue effect, and hypoglycemia, increase.

whys.A: It is not an incretin drug.
whys.B: Lower levels would cause hyperglycemia.
whys.C: The repaglinide interaction is CYP2C8.
whys.E: He has symptoms; they are not masked.

takeaway: Gemfibrozil + repaglinide = hypoglycemia.
discriminator: Same dose, higher level: an inhibitor.

stem: A 58-year-old has taken prednisone daily for 8 months for polymyalgia. He ran out 4 days ago. He presents with vomiting, weakness and blood pressure 82/50. What explains this, and what is the treatment?

options.A: Suppressed ACTH, no cortisol reserve; IV hydrocortisone
options.B: Rebound ACTH surge overdriving the adrenal; give ketoconazole
options.C: Mineralocorticoid excess from prednisone; give spironolactone
options.D: Steroid excess causing hyperglycemia; give insulin and fluids
options.E: Axis recovered within days; restart oral prednisone at home

why: Chronic steroids suppress CRH and ACTH and the adrenal shrinks. Stopping abruptly leaves the axis unable to make cortisol: adrenal crisis, treated with IV hydrocortisone and fluids. Prevention is a taper.

whys.B: ACTH is suppressed, and the adrenal has shrunk.
whys.C: Spironolactone would worsen hypotension.
whys.D: He stopped the steroid; this is deficiency.
whys.E: Recovery takes time; crisis needs IV therapy.

takeaway: Long steroid course: taper, never stop abruptly.
discriminator: Crisis = too little cortisol after suppression.

stem: A 50-year-old with Cushing syndrome needs a steroid-synthesis blocker. She takes several CYP3A4-cleared drugs and has a prolonged QT interval. A second option would raise androgens. Which pairing is correct?

options.A: Ketoconazole: gynecomastia. Metyrapone: hyperkalemia with ACE inhibitors
options.B: Ketoconazole: hypokalemia. Metyrapone: contraindicated in pregnancy
options.C: Ketoconazole: hirsutism, hypertension. Metyrapone: QT and CYP3A4 concerns
options.D: Ketoconazole: cortisol rises. Metyrapone: cortisol rises
options.E: Ketoconazole: QT and CYP3A4 concerns. Metyrapone: hirsutism, hypertension

why: Ketoconazole: hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation, strong CYP3A4 inhibition. Metyrapone raises androgens and deoxycorticosterone (hirsutism, hypertension).

whys.A: Those are spironolactone points.
whys.B: Those are mifepristone points.
whys.C: The profiles are reversed.
whys.D: Cortisol rises with mifepristone, a receptor blocker.

takeaway: Ketoconazole → liver, QT, CYP3A4. Metyrapone → androgens, blood pressure.
discriminator: Both lower cortisol; their side effects differ.

stem: A 29-year-old started methimazole 5 weeks ago for Graves disease. She calls with fever of 38.9°C and a severe sore throat for one day. Which instruction is correct?

options.A: Stop methimazole now and come in for a CBC today
options.B: Continue methimazole and check TSH in 6–8 weeks
options.C: Switch to PTU today since it has the lower liver risk
options.D: Add iodine solution to block hormone release tonight
options.E: Continue methimazole and take aspirin for the fever

why: Both thionamides carry agranulocytosis and liver warnings. Fever or sore throat on a thionamide means stop the drug and check a CBC.

whys.B: TSH timing does not address possible agranulocytosis.
whys.C: PTU has the greater liver risk and shares agranulocytosis.
whys.D: Iodine is a thyroid-storm step, not for this warning sign.
whys.E: Fever or sore throat means stop and check a CBC.

takeaway: Thionamide + fever or sore throat = stop, CBC.
discriminator: Agranulocytosis: both drugs. Worse liver risk: PTU.

stem: A 62-year-old on dialysis starts cinacalcet for secondary hyperparathyroidism. Two weeks later she has tingling around the mouth and muscle cramps. Which lab and which added risk go with this drug?

options.A: High calcium; cinacalcet also causes hypercalciuria
options.B: Low potassium; cinacalcet also causes gynecomastia
options.C: Low calcium; cinacalcet also prolongs the QT interval
options.D: High calcium; a thiazide should be added to lower it
options.E: Low sodium; cinacalcet also retains free water

why: Cinacalcet lowers PTH secretion. Adverse effects are nausea, hypocalcemia and QT prolongation, so calcium is monitored. Calcitriol and PTH replacement carry the opposite risk.

whys.A: Those are the calcitriol and PTH-replacement risks.
whys.B: That mixes mifepristone and spironolactone effects.
whys.D: Thiazides raise calcium; loops lower it.
whys.E: That is the desmopressin picture.

takeaway: Cinacalcet: watch for hypocalcemia and QT.
discriminator: Cinacalcet → low calcium; calcitriol → high calcium.

stem: A 52-year-old stable on levothyroxine starts carbamazepine for trigeminal neuralgia. Two months later his TSH is 11 mIU/L. He separates his tablet from all other products. Which mechanism fits?

options.A: Carbamazepine inhibits CYP3A4 like an azole
options.B: Carbamazepine raises thyroid-binding globulin
options.C: Carbamazepine blocks dopamine at the pituitary
options.D: Carbamazepine binds levothyroxine in the gut
options.E: Carbamazepine speeds levothyroxine clearance

why: Rifampin, phenytoin and carbamazepine speed clearance of levothyroxine and steroids.

whys.A: It is an inducer.
whys.B: That is the estrogen effect.
whys.C: That raises prolactin and is another drug class.
whys.D: He separates doses; binders are calcium, iron, antacids.

takeaway: Inducers lower levothyroxine effect.
discriminator: Spacing fixes binding; it cannot fix induction.

stem: A 63-year-old with SIADH from small-cell lung cancer has sodium 122 mEq/L and mild nausea. No therapy has been tried. Which plan matches the lecture's order of therapy?

options.A: Start tolvaptan at home and recheck sodium in two weeks
options.B: Start demeclocycline first because it has the fewest risks
options.C: Restrict fluids; tolvaptan in hospital if refractory
options.D: Start desmopressin and limit fluids to prevent water loss
options.E: Give fludrocortisone and monitor blood pressure and potassium

why: Fluid restriction is first-line for SIADH. Tolvaptan or demeclocycline are for refractory cases; tolvaptan can overcorrect sodium (osmotic demyelination) and injure the liver, so it starts in hospital.

whys.A: It is started in hospital because it can overcorrect.
whys.B: It causes photosensitivity and nephrotoxicity; not first.
whys.D: Desmopressin would retain more water.
whys.E: That is mineralocorticoid replacement, not SIADH care.

takeaway: SIADH: fluid restriction, then tolvaptan in hospital.
discriminator: DI gets desmopressin; SIADH gets restriction then a blocker.

stem: A 68-year-old with heart failure and ankle edema has A1c above goal on metformin. A colleague suggests pioglitazone. What is the main objection?

options.A: It causes the most hypoglycemia of the oral agents
options.B: Fluid retention can worsen heart failure
options.C: It causes euglycemic DKA when the patient is ill
options.D: It cannot be combined with any DPP-4 inhibitor
options.E: It causes pancreatitis and gallstones over time

why: TZDs cause fluid retention/heart failure and weight gain.

whys.A: That is the sulfonylureas.
whys.C: That is the SGLT2 inhibitors.
whys.D: That rule is for GLP-1 RAs.
whys.E: Those are GLP-1 RA concerns.

takeaway: Heart failure: no pioglitazone.
discriminator: Each class has one signature risk.

stem: A 48-year-old on a stable levothyroxine dose has TSH 9.8 mIU/L. She takes it every morning with breakfast, her calcium carbonate and a new iron tablet. She has not missed a dose. What is the best next step?

options.A: Stop the iron permanently because the two can never be combined
options.B: Switch to methimazole because the levothyroxine has failed
options.C: Increase the levothyroxine dose and recheck TSH in 2 weeks
options.D: Take it on an empty stomach, 4 h from calcium and iron
options.E: Move the dose to dinner so it is taken with the largest meal

why: Calcium, iron and antacids reduce levothyroxine absorption. Take it 30–60 minutes before breakfast and separate those products by at least 4 hours, then check TSH at 6–8 weeks.

whys.A: They can be combined when separated by 4 hours.
whys.B: Methimazole treats hyperthyroidism.
whys.C: Fix absorption first; TSH is rechecked at 6–8 weeks.
whys.E: Food reduces absorption; it is taken on an empty stomach.

takeaway: High TSH on levothyroxine: check timing before raising the dose.
discriminator: Absorption problem (binders) vs clearance problem (inducers).
